text: Hsp90 is an essential, highly abundant molecular chaperone that occupies a central position in the eukaryotic interactome and supports numerous client proteins, many implicated in cancer. Inhibition of Hsp90 compromises the accumulation of proteins that depend on it. Together with anecdotal evidence that cancer cells may be especially sensitive to Hsp90 inhibition, this property has motivated clinical trials of Hsp90 inhibitors as anticancer agents. Yet inhibitor sensitivity has not been examined in rigorously matched normal and cancer cells. Although important regulators of Hsp90 activity and inhibitor sensitivity have been identified, the basis for a possible heightened sensitivity in cancer cells remains unresolved. We addressed this question systematically by generating an isogenic pair of normal and oncogenically transformed NIH-3T3 cell lines. Proteomic analysis following treatment with three chemically distinct Hsp90 inhibitors revealed effects on a substantial fraction of the oncogenic program and confirmed hypersensitivity in transformed cells. This hypersensitivity was reversed by targeting the oncogenic signaling pathway, as well as by inhibiting DNA replication, cell growth, translation or energy metabolism. In the converse experiments, normal cells became more sensitive to Hsp90 inhibitors when stimulated with growth factors or subjected to proteostatic stress through overexpression of an aggregation-prone protein. These findings suggest that differential sensitivity to Hsp90 inhibition need not reflect a particular intrinsic distinction between normal and cancer cells. Rather, it may arise from a shift in the balance between cellular quiescence and activity, with sensitivity changing as that balance is altered.

text: We examined the post-ingestive fate of piceol and pungenol, two host-plant-derived small-molecule phenolics in the acetophenone class previously shown to be toxic to spruce budworm (Choristoneura fumiferana), an outbreaking forest pest. We tested whether these compounds undergo transformation during passage through the midgut and whether feeding on them increases activity of the detoxification enzyme glutathione-S-transferase (GST). We reared insects on foliage or artificial diet until the fourth instar, then transferred each insect individually to either a control diet or a phenolic-laced diet. After approximately 10 days of treatment, we dissected the midguts and used them to measure soluble protein by the Bradford assay and GST enzyme activity. We also collected frass for analysis by HPLC-DAD-MS. HPLC results showed that the acetophenones did not autoxidize under midgut pH conditions. However, frass from insects receiving the phenolic-laced diet contained glucose and glutathione conjugates. Insects fed this diet also showed increased GST activity in assays conducted at both neutral and alkaline pH. These findings indicate that spruce budworm mounts counter-adaptations to plant phenolics similar to those reported for angiosperm feeders. Specifically, the insects increase activity of GST, an important detoxification enzyme, and partially conjugate the ingested acetophenones before eliminating them. These responses nevertheless do not fully mitigate the toxic effects of piceol and pungenol under the conditions of our artificial-diet-based laboratory experiment. The observed conjugation and enzyme response therefore represent counter-measures whose effectiveness against the ingested compounds remains incomplete in this experimental context.

text:
Previous research has examined the reasons for the rising incidence and geographic spread of human brucellosis in mainland China, but most studies have lacked a comprehensive assessment supported by quantitative evidence. This study investigated epidemic mechanisms and associated factors to inform future countermeasures in China and elsewhere.

Provincial data on human brucellosis incidence and selected factors related to the economy, animal husbandry, transportation, health, and hygiene were collected for 2005–2016. Time series plots were used to examine annual incidence and its annual rate of change in each province. Cluster analysis then grouped all 31 mainland provinces according to their incidence time series over the study period. To accommodate the characteristics of the data, a dynamic panel data model combined with supervised principal component analysis was proposed to assess the effects of associated factors on human brucellosis.

The incidence of human brucellosis in mainland China rose approximately threefold, from 1.41 per 100,000 people in 2005 to 4.22 per 100,000 people in 2014, followed by slight declines in 2015 and 2016. Incidence remained higher in northern than in southern China throughout the study period. Southern China nevertheless showed an upward trend, particularly during 2012–2016. The 31 provinces formed three clusters, each with distinct incidence patterns over time. The estimated contribution of health and hygiene conditions to prevention and control remained very limited (regression coefficient = -0.02). This finding provided a basis for cautiously suggesting that increasing the number of medical institutions per capita and the proportion of rural medical expenditure might help prevent and control human brucellosis.

These findings indicate that the epidemiological pattern of human brucellosis in mainland China has changed across both space and time in recent years. Although incidence declined slightly after 2014, the persistent north–south difference and the increase in southern China remain relevant to control efforts. Alongside traditional control measures, greater attention should be given to improving medical care, especially in rural areas, with the aim of strengthening prevention and control. Such improvements may be helpful, although the estimated contribution of health and hygiene conditions was small.

text: Crowdfunding has become an increasingly common way to support entrepreneurial and artistic projects, but systematic evidence about its potential to fund scientific research remains limited. We begin by briefly reviewing previous crowdfunding research and surveying platforms created specifically for research crowdfunding. We then examine data from more than 700 campaigns hosted on Experiment.com, the largest dedicated platform of this kind. Our descriptive analysis characterizes the people seeking support, the projects for which they request funding, and the campaigns they conduct. We next assess how these features are associated with fundraising outcomes. The results reveal notable differences between crowdfunding and conventional research funding. Students and other junior investigators make substantial use of crowdfunding, although the projects involved are generally relatively small. Students and junior researchers are also more likely to obtain funding than senior scientists, while women achieve higher success rates than men. Traditional indicators of scientific quality, including researchers’ previous publications, show little association with campaign success. This pattern suggests that crowdfunding participants may evaluate projects using criteria that differ from those applied by established funding agencies. Overall, our findings identify meaningful opportunities for crowdfunding within science while also underscoring challenges specific to this funding model. We connect these results to scholarship on crowdfunding and the economics of science and consider their relationship to other emerging approaches that engage the public in scientific research.

text: Natural variation in the life-history traits of reef-building corals across environmental gradients remains an active area of research. We compared reproductive and genetic variability in the hermaphroditic broadcast-spawning coral Acropora hyacinthus across six latitudes in the Western Pacific: Japan (33° and 31°N), Taiwan (23°, 22°, and 21°N), and Indonesia (5°S). Corals from the lowest latitude produced significantly larger eggs than those from high-latitude populations. In contrast, mean egg number differed significantly only between the high-latitude sites and two of the three mid-latitude sites. Egg number was significantly and negatively correlated with both egg and testis volumes, indicating location-dependent reproductive trade-offs. Female gonad volumes were smaller at high latitudes and significantly greater at lower latitudes, and were positively correlated with seawater temperature. High levels of genetic similarity among most populations further indicated active gene flow across low-, mid-, and high-latitude locations. Penghu, a mid-latitude site off western Taiwan, was an exception: its population formed a distinct group characterized by highly similar genetic and reproductive traits, consistent with reproductive isolation and local adaptation. These findings document natural spatial variation in the reproductive characteristics of A. hyacinthus across latitudinally separated environments. They may therefore provide baseline information for predicting how the life histories of corals more broadly will respond to the effects of climate change.

text:
This study estimated the societal costs and patient quality of life (QoL) associated with multiple sclerosis (MS) across all disease-severity levels in Brazil, as measured by the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS).

The analysis formed part of an international, cross-sectional burden-of-illness study conducted with national MS patient organizations. Data were obtained directly from patients through a validated questionnaire. Direct costs were calculated from both societal and payer perspectives, while total costs were reported from the societal perspective.

The survey included 694 patients, with a response rate of 21% and a mean age of 40.8 years. Although 95% were of working age, only around half were employed. Mean EDSS was 3.2, and 62.5% had an EDSS score below 3. Relapses were reported by 18.9%. Fatigue affected 94% of patients across EDSS levels, while 69.1% reported cognitive difficulties. Mean utility declined from 0.77 at EDSS 0 to negative values at EDSS 9; overall mean utility was 0.58 and was also affected by relapses.

Mean annual societal cost was R$33,872 (€8,000) per patient. Direct costs accounted for 81%, equivalent to R$27,355 (€6,500), while payer direct costs were R$16,793 (€4,000) per patient.

The study population had relatively mild, early disease. Most patients had relapsing MS and were therefore receiving disease-modifying drug (DMD) treatment. Consequently, the total cost of MS in Brazil cannot be inferred directly. Nevertheless, resource use, QoL, and MS symptoms closely resembled findings from the European survey.

The double-decker bus had been converted into a motorhome and received electricity from a generator kept in a locked compartment within the vehicle. Police suspect fumes from the generator entered the living area unnoticed. Carbon monoxide has no colour or smell.

Friends discovered the problem at 2 p.m. on Saturday after going to the bus to check on the people inside. Five of the eight survivors were taken to a hospital in Stavanger, while two were transported to Ullevål University Hospital in Oslo. Three survivors remain in serious but stable condition, and two have been discharged.

Brueland and Wathne were from Oltedal in Rogaland County. Reports say they had a large extended family, whose members are caring for the couple’s children with help from friends.

The proposed overhaul would extend health benefits to more than 30 million Americans without insurance. It would also establish new rules governing the health insurance industry.

With Nelson’s backing, Democrats appeared positioned to prevail in the first of several essential procedural votes. The series was scheduled to begin at 1 a.m. Monday. If the process unfolded without delays, the Senate could hold a final vote and pass the measure on Christmas Eve.

Senate approval the following week would represent a major political victory for Obama, but it would not send the legislation immediately to his desk. The Senate bill would first have to be reconciled with a separate health care measure approved by the House of Representatives the previous month. Only after lawmakers resolved the differences between the two versions and approved a common bill could the president sign the overhaul into law the next year.

text:
In statistics, ordinary least squares (OLS) is a linear least squares technique used to select unknown parameters in a linear regression model. The model represents fixed level-one effects as a linear function of a collection of explanatory variables. OLS applies the least-squares principle: it chooses parameter values that minimize the sum of the squared differences between the observed values of the dependent variable in the input data and the values produced by the linear function of the independent variables.

Geometrically, those differences are distances measured parallel to the dependent-variable axis, running from each observed data point to its corresponding point on the regression surface. Squaring and summing the distances gives the quantity minimized by OLS; smaller differences indicate a closer fit between the model and the data. The resulting estimator has a straightforward formula, particularly for simple linear regression, where only one regressor appears on the right-hand side of the regression equation.

For level-one fixed effects, the OLS estimator is consistent when the regressors are exogenous and satisfy the rank condition by avoiding perfect collinearity. Its estimate of residual variance is consistent when the regressors have finite fourth moments. The Gauss–Markov theorem further establishes that, if the errors are homoscedastic and serially uncorrelated, OLS is optimal among linear unbiased estimators. With these conditions and finite error variances, it provides mean-unbiased estimates having minimum variance. If the errors are additionally assumed to follow a normal distribution with mean zero, OLS is also the maximum likelihood estimator and outperforms every nonlinear unbiased estimator.

text:
The British Broadcasting Corporation Microcomputer System, commonly called the BBC Micro, was a family of microcomputers and peripherals designed and manufactured by Acorn Computers during the 1980s for the BBC Computer Literacy Project. Intended primarily for education, the machines were known for robust construction, extensive expansion options, and a high-quality operating system. The Computer Programme, a related television series broadcast on BBC2 in 1982, followed presenter Chris Serle as he learned to operate the computer.

The Literacy Project invited bids for a machine that would accompany its television programmes and printed materials. Acorn secured the contract with the Proton, a successor to its Atom computer that had been prototyped at short notice. After being renamed the BBC Micro, it was adopted by most UK schools and transformed Acorn’s commercial prospects. Despite its relatively high price, it also became a successful British home computer. Acorn later used the system to simulate and develop the ARM architecture.

Nine BBC-branded models were ultimately released. In ordinary usage, however, “BBC Micro” usually denotes the first six: the Model A, B, B+64, B+128, Master 128, and Master Compact. Later BBC models are generally classified within Acorn’s Archimedes series.

text:
Selective breeding, or artificial selection, is the process through which people develop particular phenotypic traits in animals and plants by deciding which males and females will reproduce together. Domesticated animals are classified as breeds and are ordinarily bred by professional breeders. Domesticated plants may be described as varieties, cultigens, cultivars, or breeds. When two purebred animals belonging to different breeds reproduce, their offspring are crossbreeds; comparable crosses between plants are called hybrids. Amateurs, commercial professionals, and non-commercial professionals may breed flowers, vegetables, and fruit trees, although major crops generally originate with professional breeders.

Animal breeders employ methods including inbreeding, linebreeding, and outcrossing, while plant breeders use similar approaches. In his 1859 book On the Origin of Species, Charles Darwin examined the success of selective breeding in producing changes over time. text:
The Slavic languages, also called the Slavonic languages, belong to the Indo-European language family. They are spoken mainly by Slavic peoples and their descendants. Scholars generally believe that they developed from Proto-Slavic, a reconstructed language spoken during the Early Middle Ages. Proto-Slavic is itself thought to have descended from the older Proto-Balto-Slavic language. This ancestry connects Slavic with the Baltic languages, forming the Balto-Slavic branch of Indo-European.

Slavic languages are conventionally divided into East, West, and South subgroups, although this classification also reflects factors outside language itself. Together, the three groups contain more than 20 languages. Ten have at least one million speakers and serve as official national languages in the countries where they are mainly spoken. The East Slavic group includes Russian, Belarusian, and Ukrainian. Polish, Czech, and Slovak belong to the West Slavic group. Among the South Slavic languages, Bulgarian and Macedonian developed from eastern dialects, while Serbo-Croatian and Slovene developed from western dialects. The linguist Aleksandr Dulichenko also recognizes several Slavic microlanguages, including isolated ethnolects as well as peripheral dialects of better-established Slavic languages.

Today, native Slavic-language communities extend across the Balkans and Central and Eastern Europe, and eastward from Western Siberia to the Russian Far East. Migration has also created isolated minority communities of Slavic-language speakers throughout the world. At the beginning of the twenty-first century, the combined number of speakers of all Slavic languages was estimated at 315 million. Taken together, they form Europe’s largest ethnolinguistic group.

This study estimated societal costs and patients’ quality of life (QoL) across multiple sclerosis (MS) severity levels in Brazil, measured using the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS).

Mean EDSS was 3.2, with 62.5% scoring <3. Relapses were reported by 18.9%. Fatigue affected 94%, irrespective of EDSS level, and 69.1% reported cognitive difficulties. Mean utility ranged from 0.77 at EDSS 0 to negative values at EDSS 9, averaging 0.58 overall; relapses affected utility. Mean annual societal cost per patient was R$33,872 (€8,000). The sample represented relatively mild, early disease. Most patients had relapsing disease and were therefore receiving disease-modifying drug (DMD) treatment. These findings do not permit a direct conclusion about the total cost of MS in Brazil. Nevertheless, the quantities of resources used, QoL and MS symptoms were very similar to those observed in the European survey, despite the limits on drawing conclusions about total national costs from this study population.

The collapse happened at 10:00 a.m. local time during classes at College La Promesse Evangelique in Pétionville, a suburb of Port-au-Prince. Reports say construction was underway on the third floor, although it is not known whether that work caused the collapse.

At least 700 children were attending the school when the building fell. The school taught pupils from kindergarten through secondary grades, with students ranging in age from 3 to 20.

The building reportedly suffered a partial collapse eight years earlier. Residents nearby moved away because they feared the remaining structure would fall onto their homes. Following that earlier collapse, the school's owner tried to purchase the homes and properties around the school. The cause of Friday's collapse remains unknown.

The agreement marks a breakthrough in their effort to advance President Barack Obama’s leading domestic priority.

Senators gathered in Washington on Saturday amid a driving snowstorm, working urgently toward their self-imposed Christmas deadline. Nelson, a conservative Democrat also described as a moderate, had been the last senator withholding the support Democrats needed as they confronted determined Republican resistance and a shrinking legislative timetable.

Nelson said he agreed to back the measure after Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid offered further concessions. Those included restrictions on the availability of abortions through insurance sold under the legislation, as well as millions of dollars in Medicaid funding for Nebraska. His decision supplied the crucial 60th vote Democrats had been seeking.

The proposed legislation would provide health benefits to more than 30 million Americans who lack insurance. It would also place new regulatory requirements on the health insurance industry.

With Nelson’s backing, Democrats should be able to win the first in a series of important procedural votes, scheduled to start at 1 a.m. Monday. If the process proceeds smoothly, the sequence would end with a final vote approving the bill on Christmas Eve, ahead of the December 25 deadline.

Senate passage next week would be seen as a major victory for Obama, though it would leave another legislative step unfinished. The Senate measure would have to be reconciled with the health care reform bill approved by the House of Representatives last month before the president could sign the resulting legislation into law next year.

Ellery and his father must pursue their inquiry while also fighting the fire that threatens everyone in the house. Fourteen-year-old Elliot Sutton moves to a new town and starts at a school where no one knows him. He wants to attract just enough attention to belong without making himself a target. At first, his reinvention succeeds. But its success soon takes him further than he intended.

Elliot is no longer being bullied, yet he’s quickly drawn toward the Guardians, a secret society of older boys responsible for a reign of terror at his new school. When they summon him, he assumes they’ve seen through his carefully constructed disguise. Instead, they’re impressed by the person he appears to be and want him to join their ranks.

The story follows Elliot as he tries to work out how to escape this predicament. He has managed to get away from his traumatic past, but the future now taking shape threatens to turn him into a Guardian—and one of the very bullies he used to despise.

text: Unlike Ballard’s earlier novel The Drowned World, The Burning World depicts a world starved of water. A prolonged drought reduces rivers to trickles and turns the land to dust, driving people worldwide toward the oceans to find water. Industrial waste dumped at sea causes the drought: it forms a barrier of saturated long-chain polymers that lets oxygen through but stops evaporation, destroying the precipitation cycle. Since the novel’s publication, plastic islands, including the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, have been discovered across vast stretches of the world’s oceans. Their effects on ocean evaporation and the precipitation cycle have not been studied, leaving the relationship between these real accumulations and the novel’s imagined disaster unexamined.

text:
Ordinary least squares (OLS) is a statistical method within the broader family of linear least squares methods. It estimates unknown parameters in a linear regression model whose level-one effects are fixed and whose fitted function is linear in a set of explanatory variables. The parameters are chosen by minimizing the sum of squared differences between the dependent-variable values observed in the input dataset and the values produced by the linear function of the independent variables.

The geometric interpretation concerns distances from data points to the regression surface. For each observation, the distance to its corresponding point on that surface is measured parallel to the dependent-variable axis. OLS minimizes the sum of these squared distances, with smaller differences indicating a closer fit to the data. A simple formula expresses the resulting estimator; it is particularly straightforward for simple linear regression, where the regression equation has just one regressor on its right-hand side.

The estimator is consistent for the level-one fixed effects when the regressors are exogenous and form perfect collinearity, expressed as a rank condition. Consistency of the residual variance estimate requires regressors with finite fourth moments. Under the Gauss–Markov theorem, OLS is optimal among linear unbiased estimators when errors are homoscedastic and serially uncorrelated. Given these conditions and finite error variances, OLS yields mean-unbiased estimates with minimum variance within that class.

If the errors are additionally assumed to follow a normal distribution with zero mean, OLS is also the maximum likelihood estimator. With this further distributional assumption, its advantage extends beyond linear unbiased estimation: it outperforms any nonlinear unbiased estimator.

text:
The British Broadcasting Corporation Microcomputer System, commonly called the BBC Micro, comprises a series of microcomputers and related peripherals that Acorn Computers designed and manufactured during the 1980s for the BBC Computer Literacy Project. Its educational design emphasised durability, expansion capabilities and a high-quality operating system. In 1982, BBC2 broadcast an accompanying television series, The Computer Programme, in which Chris Serle learned to use the computer.

The Literacy Project invited bids for a computer to support its television programmes and literature. Acorn secured the contract with the Proton, a successor to its Atom computer that it had prototyped at short notice. Under its new name, BBC Micro, the machine reached most schools in the United Kingdom, transforming Acorn’s fortunes. It also sold successfully in the UK home computer market despite its high price. Acorn subsequently used the BBC Micro to simulate and develop the ARM architecture.

Nine models ultimately carried BBC branding, although in everyday usage “BBC Micro” generally denotes the first six: Model A, B, B+64, B+128, Master 128 and Master Compact. The later BBC-branded models are regarded as members of Acorn’s Archimedes series.

text:
Selective breeding, also known as artificial selection, involves humans choosing which individuals, typically male and female animals or plants, reproduce sexually together to develop particular phenotypic traits, or characteristics, in their offspring. Domesticated animal groups are called breeds and are normally bred by professional breeders. Domesticated plants are described as varieties, cultigens, cultivars, or breeds. The offspring of two purebred animals belonging to different breeds is a crossbreed; crossbred plants are termed hybrids. The Slavic, or Slavonic, languages belong to the Indo-European family and are spoken mainly by Slavic peoples and their descendants. They are believed to have developed from Proto-Slavic, a common ancestral language spoken in the Early Middle Ages. Proto-Slavic is itself thought to have come from the older Proto-Balto-Slavic language. This proposed ancestry connects the Slavic and Baltic languages in a Balto-Slavic group within the broader Indo-European family.

The conventional classification divides Slavic languages into three subgroups: East, South and West. This division draws partly on features outside language itself. Together, the subgroups contain more than 20 languages. Ten have at least one million speakers each and hold official status as national languages in the countries where they are mainly spoken. The East Slavic languages in this category are Russian, Belarusian and Ukrainian; the West Slavic languages are Polish, Czech and Slovak. Within South Slavic, Bulgarian and Macedonian belong to the eastern dialects, while Serbo-Croatian and Slovene belong to the western dialects. Aleksandr Dulichenko also recognizes several Slavic microlanguages. These include both isolated ethnolects—language varieties associated with ethnic groups—and peripheral dialects of more established Slavic languages.

Today, native speakers of Slavic languages are found in the Balkans and across Central and Eastern Europe, as well as throughout the area stretching from Western Siberia to the Russian Far East. Diasporas of many Slavic peoples have also formed isolated minority communities of speakers around the world. At the beginning of the twenty-first century, the combined number of speakers of Slavic languages was estimated at 315 million. They make up Europe’s largest ethnolinguistic group.

Research on the rising incidence and geographic spread of human brucellosis in mainland China has generally proceeded without comprehensive quantitative evidence. This study examined the epidemic mechanism of human brucellosis and the factors associated with it, with the aim of informing future countermeasures in China and elsewhere.

Provincial-level data covering 2005–2016 were assembled on human brucellosis incidence and on associated factors spanning economy, animal husbandry, transportation, and health and hygiene. Annual incidence and annual rate of change were first displayed as time series plots for each province. Cluster analysis then grouped all 31 provinces of mainland China according to their incidence series over the study period. Given the structure of the data, a dynamic panel data model combined with supervised principal component analysis was proposed to estimate the effects of the associated factors.

Incidence rose three-fold, from 1.41 per 100,000 people in 2005 to 4.22 per 100,000 people in 2014, with a slight decline in 2015 and 2016. Rates in northern provinces have consistently exceeded those in the south, although southern provinces also trended upward, particularly between 2012 and 2016. The 31 provinces fell into three clusters, each with a distinct incidence trajectory. The contribution of health and hygiene conditions to prevention and control remained limited and trivial in magnitude (regression coefficient = −0.02). On this basis it is plausible to suppose that raising the per-person number of medical institutes and the proportion of rural medical expenditure could assist prevention and control of human brucellosis.

The epidemic status of human brucellosis in mainland China has shifted along both spatial and temporal dimensions in recent years. The northern predominance persists, but the southern upward trend indicates that the disease is no longer confined to its traditional high-burden regions, and the three-cluster structure suggests that provinces do not follow a single epidemic pattern. Alongside conventional control measures directed at animal husbandry and transmission, greater attention to medical healthcare provision, particularly in rural areas, is warranted as a means of strengthening control.

This paper starts with a brief review of prior work on crowdfunding and a survey of the platforms built specifically for funding research. We then turn to data from more than 700 campaigns hosted on Experiment.com, the largest of these dedicated platforms. Our descriptive analysis sheds light on three things: who the creators seeking funding are, what kinds of projects they're pitching, and how the campaigns themselves are run. We next ask how those characteristics relate to whether a campaign succeeds. The results point to meaningful differences between crowdfunding and the traditional funding channels available to researchers. Students and other junior investigators make heavy use of the platform, though the projects tend to be relatively small; those same students and junior investigators are more likely to succeed than senior scientists, and women succeed at higher rates than men. Conventional quality signals, including a scientist's publication record, show little relationship with funding success, which suggests the crowd may be weighing different criteria than traditional funding agencies do. We read these findings as evidence of real opportunity alongside distinctive challenges, connecting them to the economics of science, to crowdfunding research, and to other emerging ways of involving the public in science.

text: How the life history traits of reef-building corals vary naturally across environmental gradients remains an active research question. Here we examine variability in reproductive and genetic characteristics of Acropora hyacinthus, a hermaphroditic broadcast spawner, sampled from the Western Pacific Region at six latitudes: two sites in Japan (33° and 31°N), three in Taiwan (23°, 22° and 21°N), and one in Indonesia (5°S). Corals at the lowest latitude sampled produced eggs that were significantly larger than those from high-latitude sites, whereas mean egg number differed significantly only between the high-latitude location and two of the three mid-latitude locations. Egg number showed a significant negative correlation with both egg volume and testis volume, evidence of reproductive trade-offs operating across locations. Female gonad volumes were reduced at high latitudes and significantly greater at lower latitudes, and were positively correlated with seawater temperature. Genetic similarity among populations was high, implying ongoing gene flow linking low-, mid- and high-latitude sites. Penghu, a mid-latitude location off western Taiwan, departed from this pattern: it formed an independent cluster characterised by strongly similar genetic and reproductive traits, which points to reproductive isolation accompanied by local adaptation. By documenting natural spatial variation in the reproductive traits of A. hyacinthus across a latitudinal range, this study provides baseline information for predicting how coral life histories more broadly may respond to climate change impacts.

text:
This study set out to measure the cost of multiple sclerosis to society and the quality of life of patients across the full range of disease severity in Brazil, with severity graded by the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS). The work formed one arm of an international cross-sectional burden-of-illness study conducted together with national MS patient organizations. Patients supplied all of the information themselves through a validated questionnaire. Direct costs were calculated from two viewpoints, that of society and that of the payer; total costs are reported as societal costs.

Responses came from 694 patients, a response rate of 21%, with a mean age of 40.8 years. Ninety-five percent were of working age and roughly half held jobs. The mean EDSS score was 3.2, and 62.5% of patients scored below 3. Relapses were reported by 18.9%. Fatigue was near-universal, affecting 94% of patients at every EDSS level, and 69.1% reported cognitive difficulties. Mean utility fell from 0.77 at EDSS 0 to negative values at EDSS 9, averaging 0.58 overall, and relapses lowered it further. From the societal perspective, the mean total annual cost came to R$33,872 (€8,000) per patient, of which direct costs made up 81% (R$27,355, €6,500). Direct costs to the payer were R$16,793 (€4,000) per patient.

The sample had relatively mild, early disease, mostly relapsing and therefore receiving DMD treatment, so no direct conclusion can be drawn about the total cost of MS in Brazil. Even so, resource use, quality of life and symptoms closely resembled findings from the European survey.

More information has come out about the two people who died at the annual Norway Rock Festival in Kvinesdal. Eight others were pulled unconscious from a bus at the site. British heavy metal band Motörhead began their festival set with a minute's silence for the dead, according to reports.

Police have released the names of the victims: Terje Brueland, 32, and Anita Wathne, 31. As reported earlier, the two were an unmarried couple and leave behind three children. Carbon monoxide poisoning is believed to have caused the deaths.

Investigators found that the double-decker bus had been converted into a motorhome. Its electricity came from a generator kept in a locked compartment on the vehicle. Police think fumes from the generator seeped inside without being detected, since carbon monoxide has no smell or colour.

Friends who went to the bus to check on the people inside found the problem at 2 p.m. Saturday. Of the eight survivors, five were taken to hospital in Stavanger and two to Ullevål University Hospital in Oslo. Three are still in serious but stable condition, and two have been discharged.

The couple who died came from Oltedal in Rogaland County. They are reported to have a large family there, and relatives, along with friends, are now caring for their children.

At least 82 people are now known to have died in the collapse of a school in Haiti on Friday. The toll climbed from 61 after rescuers pulled 20 students and their teacher from a space between two of the building's floors. Another 200 or more are feared to be trapped, and over 100 people were hurt, some of them badly.

According to reports, work was under way on the third floor of the College La Promesse Evangelique in Pétionville, a suburb of Port-au-Prince, when the building came down. Whether that construction caused the collapse is not known. The building fell at 10:00 a.m. local time, during the school day.

At least 700 children were in the school at the time. They ranged from kindergarten pupils to secondary students, and their ages ranged from 3 to 20.

Part of the school is said to have collapsed eight years ago. People living nearby moved away then, afraid the remaining structure would fall onto their homes. After that earlier collapse, the school's owner tried to buy up the surrounding houses and land.

text:
Senate Democrats have secured the 60th vote they need to push a sweeping health care overhaul past fierce Republican opposition, breaking a deadlock that had stalled President Barack Obama's top domestic priority. The decisive commitment came from a conservative Democrat.

Senators worked through Saturday in Washington, D.C., as a driving snowstorm hit the capital, scrambling to move the legislation forward. Attention centered on Ben Nelson of Nebraska, a moderate Democrat and the last holdout in his party's caucus. Democrats were racing both the clock and determined Republican resistance, having set themselves a deadline of December 25th — Christmas Day — to pass the bill.

Nelson said he agreed to back the measure after extracting fresh concessions from Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid. Those include restrictions on the availability of abortion coverage in insurance plans sold under the new law, along with millions of dollars in Medicaid money for Nebraska.

The bill would extend health benefits to more than 30 million uninsured Americans and place new regulations on the health insurance industry.

With Nelson on board, Democrats expect to clear the first in a series of crucial procedural votes, the earliest of which is scheduled for one o'clock Monday morning. If nothing goes wrong for them, that sequence would end with final passage on Christmas Eve.

Getting a bill through the Senate next week would count as a significant win for Obama, though it would not be the end of the process. The Senate measure would still have to be reconciled with the health care legislation the House of Representatives approved last month. Only after the two chambers settle on a single version could the president sign it, something that would not happen until next year.

text: On vacation, Ellery Queen and his father find themselves driving through mountain country in the United States when a forest fire blocks their route and drives them to take refuge in a private house perched on a summit. Before long the blaze makes leaving impossible. The retreat belongs to Dr. Xavier, and it shelters a strange collection of people: the doctor's family, his guests, a pair of teenage boys who are conjoined — "Siamese" — xiphopagous twins, an assistant nicknamed "Bones" who is forever burying mysterious parcels on the grounds, and a further refugee who insists on being called "Mr. Smith." As the fire climbs toward them, the doctor is murdered, and afterward his brother. Each body is discovered gripping half of a playing card, and one such fragment — half a jack of diamonds — appears to point at one, and strictly one, of the conjoined twins as the killer. The narrow field of suspects also takes in a kleptomaniac whose thefts are confined to rings, and a blackmailer. Father and son must pursue the murders while simultaneously fighting the encroaching flames. Ellery carries out a long, elaborate piece of reasoning concerning the murderer's handedness, drawn entirely from the way the cards were torn. The answer to both killings emerges in a dramatic climax, just as the fire reaches the mountaintop.

text:
Inventing Elliot asks what happens when a teenager decides, deliberately, to become someone else. Elliot Sutton is fourteen, and the move to a new town and a new school — somewhere nobody knows his history — looks like his chance to shed years of being bullied and begin again. It isn't really that, though. Worn down by being the victim, he sets about remaking himself: small adjustments to how he looks, and a performance of confidence and coolness he doesn't actually feel. The goal he sets himself is to stand out just enough to fit in.

The plan works. That's the problem — it works too well. Elliot is no longer anybody's target, but he finds himself drawn quickly into the shadow of the Guardians, a secret society of older boys running a campaign of terror through the school. When they call him in, Elliot assumes his disguise has slipped and he's been found out. The reality is nearly the opposite: the Guardians are impressed by the persona he's built, and they want him to join them.

From there, the novel traces Elliot's attempt to find a way out of the trap he's made for himself. He has escaped his painful past, but the future taking shape in front of him is membership in the Guardians — becoming one of the bullies he once despised.

text:
Ordinary least squares, usually abbreviated OLS, belongs to the family of linear least squares methods in statistics. Its job is to pin down the unknown parameters of a linear regression model — one with fixed level-one effects of a linear function of a set of explanatory variables — and it does so by following the least squares principle. That principle says: take the observed values of the dependent variable in the input dataset, subtract what the linear function of the independent variable predicts, square each of those differences, and pick the parameters that make the total as small as possible.

There is a picture behind the arithmetic. Imagine the squared distances running parallel to the dependent variable's axis, each one stretching from a data point to the matching point on the regression surface. Shrinking those distances is what fitting the model means; the smaller they are, the better the fit. What comes out of the procedure can be written as a simple formula, and it is simplest of all for simple linear regression, where only one regressor sits on the right-hand side of the equation.

The estimator's properties come with conditions attached. It is consistent for the level-one fixed effects provided the regressors are exogenous and form perfect colinearity — the rank condition. It is consistent for the variance estimate of the residuals when the regressors have finite fourth moments. The Gauss–Markov theorem adds that OLS is optimal among linear unbiased estimators when the errors are homoscedastic and serially uncorrelated; given errors with finite variances, it delivers minimum-variance mean-unbiased estimation. Assume further that the errors are normally distributed with zero mean, and OLS becomes the maximum likelihood estimator, outperforming any non-linear unbiased estimator.

text:
The BBC Micro, formally the British Broadcasting Corporation Microcomputer System, was a line of microcomputers and peripherals that Acorn Computers designed and manufactured during the 1980s for the BBC Computer Literacy Project. Education shaped its design, and it earned a reputation for durable construction, room for expansion, and a well-regarded operating system. BBC2 broadcast a companion television series in 1982, The Computer Programme, in which Chris Serle learned to operate the machine.

The Literacy Project invited bids for a computer to accompany its programmes and printed material. Acorn secured the contract with the Proton, a successor to its Atom that the company prototyped on short notice. Rebranded as the BBC Micro, it was taken up by most schools in the United Kingdom and transformed Acorn's commercial position. It also sold well as a home computer in Britain, even though it was expensive. Acorn went on to use the machine to simulate and develop the ARM architecture.

Nine models eventually carried the BBC name, but in ordinary usage "BBC Micro" refers to the first six: the Model A, Model B, B+64, B+128, Master 128, and Master Compact. Later BBC-branded models are counted within Acorn's Archimedes series.

text:
Selective breeding, also known as artificial selection, refers to the human practice of developing particular phenotypic traits — that is, observable characteristics — in animals and plants by determining which males and females will mate and produce offspring. In animals, the resulting domesticated populations are called breeds, and they are usually maintained by a professional breeder. Domesticated plants go by several names: varieties, cultigens, cultivars, or breeds. When two purebred animals from different breeds are mated, the offspring is a crossbreed; the plant equivalent, produced by crossing, is termed a hybrid. Amateurs as well as commercial and non-commercial professionals may breed flowers, vegetables, and fruit-trees, though the major crops generally fall to professionals.

Animal breeders draw on techniques including inbreeding, linebreeding, and outcrossing, and comparable methods appear in plant breeding. Charles Darwin took up the subject in the opening chapter of On the Origin of Species (1859), examining the selective breeding and domestication of pigeons, cats, cattle, and dogs, and pointing to the changes such breeding had achieved over time. He treated artificial selection as a starting point from which to introduce and argue for his theory of natural selection.

Today the deliberate use of selective breeding to obtain desired outcomes is widespread in agriculture and in experimental biology.

Not all selective breeding is intentional. It can arise incidentally from human cultivation, and it can yield unintended consequences, whether welcome or unwelcome. In certain grains, for instance, seeds may have grown larger because of particular ploughing practices rather than because anyone deliberately chose the larger seeds. The domestication of plants most likely reflects an interdependence between natural and artificial factors rather than either acting alone.

text:
Optical sorting — you'll also hear it called digital sorting — is the automated business of sorting solid products with cameras, lasers, or both. What a sorter can actually detect depends on which sensors it uses and on how much intelligence the software behind the image processing brings to the job: color, size, shape, structural properties, and chemical composition are all within reach. The machine then measures each object against accept/reject criteria that the user has defined, and uses that comparison either to pull defective products and foreign material (FM) off the production line, or to separate product into different grades or material types.

One of the technology's real advantages is that the inspection is non-destructive and covers 100 percent of the flow, in-line and at full production volumes.

Food processors around the world rely on optical sorters, with adoption highest in harvested foods such as potatoes, fruits, vegetables, and nuts. Pharmaceutical and nutraceutical manufacturing, tobacco processing, waste recycling, and other industries use it too. Set against manual sorting, which is subjective and inconsistent, it improves quality, maximizes throughput, and raises yields while cutting labor costs.

text:
The Slavic languages, sometimes called the Slavonic languages, belong to the Indo-European family and are spoken mainly by the Slavic peoples and their descendants. Scholars believe they all go back to a single parent tongue, Proto-Slavic, which was spoken during the Early Middle Ages. Proto-Slavic itself is thought to descend from a still older language, Proto-Balto-Slavic, and that connection is what ties the Slavic languages to the Baltic ones within a Balto-Slavic branch of Indo-European.

By convention — a grouping that also takes extralinguistic features into account — the family is split into three subgroups: East, South, and West. Together these cover more than twenty languages. Ten of them have at least a million speakers each and serve as official national languages in the countries where they are chiefly spoken. The East group contributes Russian, Belarusian, and Ukrainian; the West group Polish, Czech, and Slovak; and the South group four more, with Bulgarian and Macedonian belonging to its eastern dialects and Serbo-Croatian and Slovene to its western ones. Beyond these, Aleksandr Dulichenko identifies a set of Slavic microlanguages, a category that takes in both isolated ethnolects and outlying dialects of better-established Slavic languages.

Today, Slavic languages are spoken natively across the Balkans, throughout Central and Eastern Europe, and in a broad stretch reaching from Western Siberia to the Russian Far East. On top of that, emigration has scattered small communities of speakers across the globe, wherever Slavic diasporas have settled. Around the turn of the twenty-first century, the total number of speakers of all Slavic languages combined was estimated at 315 million, making them the largest ethno-linguistic group in Europe.

text: In mathematics, a basis function is one element of a chosen basis for a function space. Every function in that space can be written as a linear combination of basis functions, in the same way that every vector in a vector space can be written as a linear combination of basis vectors. Numerical analysts and approximation theorists also call these blending functions, a name that comes from their role in interpolation. There, a mixture of the basis functions yields an interpolating function, and the particular "blend" depends on how the basis functions evaluate at the data points.

Arnold Hodgkiss, a jewel thief, travels to London intending to steal the Crown Jewels. While he dreamily sizes up the Tower of London, a strange man walks up to him and announces, "The crown is large." Hodgkiss, thrown by this, answers "And very heavy" — and without knowing it, gives the correct countersign. The man, a spy, shoves a parcel into his hands and vanishes. Hodgkiss holds on to the package, figuring he can turn it to his own profit somehow.

Not long after, Jerry Cornell draws a new assignment: find the stolen plans for "Project Glass." The authorities have caught the thief, but the plans remain missing, and everyone assumes a fiendish Chinese agent named Kung Fu Tzu has them. text:
Ordinary least squares, commonly abbreviated OLS, belongs to the family of linear least squares techniques used in statistics to estimate the unknown parameters of a linear regression model, where the level-one effects of a linear function of explanatory variables are treated as fixed. The underlying idea is the least squares principle itself: the parameters are chosen so as to minimize the sum of squared differences between the dependent variable's observed values in the dataset and the values predicted by the linear function of the independent variable.

Viewed geometrically, this amounts to minimizing the sum of squared distances—measured parallel to the axis of the dependent variable—between each data point and its corresponding point on the regression surface. A closer fit between the two means smaller differences, and therefore a better-fitting model. When the regression involves just one regressor on the right-hand side, as in simple linear regression, the resulting estimator takes on a particularly straightforward formula.

Several conditions govern the quality of the OLS estimator. It is consistent for the fixed effects at level one provided the regressors are exogenous and avoid perfect collinearity, satisfying what is known as the rank condition. It is likewise consistent in estimating the variance of the residuals as long as the regressors possess finite fourth moments. Furthermore, the Gauss–Markov theorem establishes that OLS is optimal among linear unbiased estimators whenever the errors are homoscedastic and free of serial correlation—conditions under which OLS achieves minimum-variance, mean-unbiased estimation, so long as the errors have finite variance. Should the errors also be normally distributed with a mean of zero, OLS becomes the maximum likelihood estimator, surpassing even non-linear unbiased alternatives in performance.

text:
Selective breeding, sometimes termed artificial selection, refers to the practice by which people direct animal and plant breeding toward particular phenotypic traits, by choosing which males and females are permitted to reproduce together. Among domesticated animals, the resulting populations are called breeds and are usually managed by professional breeders; domesticated plants are similarly termed varieties, cultigens, cultivars, or breeds. When two purebred animals of differing breeds are mated, the offspring is described as a crossbreed, while the plant equivalent is known as a hybrid. Although amateurs and both commercial and non-commercial professionals may breed flowers, vegetables, and fruit trees, the major agricultural crops are generally the domain of professional breeders.

Animal breeders rely on methods such as inbreeding, linebreeding, and outcrossing, and comparable techniques are applied in plant breeding. Charles Darwin examined the effectiveness of selective breeding in bringing about change over time in his 1859 work, On the Origin of Species, whose opening chapter treats the selective breeding and domestication of animals including pigeons, cats, cattle, and dogs. Darwin used this discussion of artificial selection as a foundation for introducing and supporting his theory of natural selection.

The deliberate use of selective breeding to achieve desired outcomes is now widespread throughout agriculture and experimental biology.

At the same time, selective breeding need not be intentional: it can arise as a byproduct of ordinary human cultivation and may yield unintended consequences, whether beneficial or harmful. In certain grains, for instance, larger seed size may have emerged from particular ploughing practices rather than from any deliberate choice to favor bigger seeds. It is likely, then, that natural and artificial influences have acted together, in mutual dependence, to shape the domestication of plants.

text:
Optical sorting, sometimes known as digital sorting, is an automated way of sorting solid products with the help of cameras and lasers. Depending on what kind of sensors are involved and how sophisticated the image-processing software is, these sorters can pick up on an object's color, size, shape, structural traits and even its chemical makeup. The machine checks each item against criteria set by the user, so it can pull out defective goods or foreign material from a production line, or separate items by grade or material type. One of the big advantages is that it does this non-destructively, inspecting every single item in-line even while running at full production speed.

You'll find optical sorters used heavily in the food industry worldwide, especially for harvested foods like potatoes, fruits, vegetables and nuts, again with that non-destructive, 100 percent in-line inspection at full volume. The technology also shows up in pharmaceutical and nutraceutical manufacturing, tobacco processing, and waste recycling, among other fields. Compared with manual sorting, which tends to be subjective and inconsistent, optical sorting helps boost product quality, push throughput higher, increase yields, and cut down on labor costs.

text:
The Slavic languages, sometimes called the Slavonic languages, belong to the Indo-European family and are spoken mainly by Slavic peoples and their descendants around the world. Scholars believe they developed from a single ancestor language, Proto-Slavic, used during the Early Middle Ages. That language, in turn, is thought to have grown out of an earlier tongue, Proto-Balto-Slavic, which is why the Slavic languages are grouped together with the Baltic languages under the wider Balto-Slavic branch of Indo-European.

By convention, and partly based on factors outside language itself, the Slavic languages are split into three groups: East, South, and West. Altogether these branches include more than twenty languages. Ten of them have at least a million speakers each and serve as official national languages: Russian, Belarusian, and Ukrainian in the East group; Polish, Czech, and Slovak in the West group; and, within the South group, Bulgarian and Macedonian (its eastern dialects) along with Serbo-Croatian and Slovene (its western dialects). Beyond these, linguist Aleksandr Dulichenko also identifies a set of Slavic microlanguages, made up of both standalone ethnolects and smaller dialects tied to larger, more firmly established Slavic languages.

Today, native speakers of Slavic languages are found across the Balkans, Central and Eastern Europe, and eastward through Western Siberia to the Russian Far East. Emigration has also carried Slavic speakers to many other parts of the world, creating scattered minority communities elsewhere. Around the start of the twenty-first century, the combined number of Slavic-language speakers was estimated at about 315 million, making Slavic the largest ethno-linguistic group in Europe.

text: A basis function is a member of a particular basis for a function space. Mathematicians can represent every function in that space as a linear combination of these basis functions, much as they represent every vector in a vector space as a linear combination of basis vectors. Numerical analysts and approximation theorists sometimes call basis functions "blending functions" instead, reflecting how interpolation uses them: combining, or blending, the basis functions produces an interpolating function, with the particular blend determined by evaluating those functions at the given data points.

text: Arnold Hodgkiss, a jewel thief, arrives in London to steal the Crown Jewels and idles near the Tower of London, sizing up the place. A stranger approaches him there and says, "The crown is large." Caught off guard, Hodgkiss answers, "And very heavy," unaware that he has just given the correct countersign. The stranger, actually a spy, shoves a parcel into his hands and vanishes. Hodgkiss holds onto it, hoping he can somehow profit from the mix-up. Soon after, Jerry Cornell gets a new assignment: track down the missing plans for "Project Glass." The original thief has been caught, but the plans remain missing, and officials suspect a ruthless Chinese agent, Kung Fu Tzu, has them. In fact, Kung never received the plans at all; they landed with Hodgkiss by mistake, leaving Kung furious. The comedy of errors builds as Cornell pursues Kung, who is meanwhile shadowing Hodgkiss. Hodgkiss manages to shake Kung off, only to run into fresh trouble when he attempts to steal a brooch from a stall on Portobello Road.
